children.translated_text: This is nothing but <s>vijñaptimātra</s> (representation-only), because unreal objects appear,
just as one suffering from an eye disorder sees unreal hairs, moons, and the like.
If representation does not arise from an object, there would be no restriction of place and time, no restriction among streams of consciousness,

children.text: na ca kṛtyakriyā yuktā vijñaptiryadi nārthataḥ ||
children.translated_text: and the performance of an effective action would not be coherent.
Restriction of place and so forth is established as in a dream; moreover, as among hungry ghosts,
there is no restriction to one stream when all of them see rivers of pus and the like.
The performance of an effective action is established as with injury in a dream, and moreover as in hell,
where wardens of hell and the like are seen and torment the inhabitants.

children.text: tiraścāṃ saṃbhavaḥ svarge yathā ca narake tathā
children.translated_text: Just as animals can be born in heaven, so too could they be born in hell.

children.text: na pretānāṃ yatastajjaṃ duḥkhaṃ nānubhavanti te ||
children.translated_text: No, for those wardens are not among the hungry ghosts, since they do not experience the suffering produced there.
If it is accepted that, through their actions, the elements arise there
and undergo such transformation, why is a transformation of consciousness not accepted?
The latent impression of an action is imagined in one place and its result in another.

children.text: tatraiva neṣyate yatra vāsanā kiṃ nu kāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Why indeed is the result not accepted precisely where the latent impression resides?
The existence of the sense fields of form and so forth was taught for the sake of people to be disciplined by that teaching,
by force of an underlying intention, just like the teaching of spontaneously born beings.

children.text: nāstīha sattva ātmā vā dharmāstvete sahetukāḥ
children.translated_text: There is no being or self here; rather, there are only these causally conditioned <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena).
For when a representation arising from its own seed proceeds with the appearance of those things,
the Sage called them the twofold sense field.
For in this way there is entry into the selflessness of the person; in another way, moreover,
the teaching provides entry into the selflessness of <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena) with respect to their imagined nature.

children.text: na tadekaṃ na cānekaṃ viṣayaḥ paramāṇuśaḥ
children.translated_text: The object is neither one nor many: it is not perceived atom by atom,

children.text: na ca te saṃhatā yasmātparamāṇurna sidhyati ||
children.translated_text: nor are the atoms perceived as an aggregate, since an atom itself cannot be established.
Because an atom connects simultaneously with six others, it would have six parts;
but if the six occupy the same location, the aggregate would be only the size of one atom.
If atoms do not make contact, whose contact exists in their aggregate?
Nor can their contact be established on the ground that they have no parts.
Whatever has distinct parts facing different directions cannot coherently be a unity.

children.text: chāyāvṛtī kathaṃ vā anyo na piṇḍaś cen na tasya te ||
children.translated_text: Otherwise, how could shadow and obstruction occur? If the aggregate is not distinct from the atoms, those two cannot belong to it.

children.text: ekatve na krameṇetir yugapan na grahāgrahau
children.translated_text: If the object were a unity, there would be no gradual movement across it, nor simultaneous apprehension and non-apprehension,
nor its occurrence in many separated places, nor failure to see its subtle parts.

children.text: pratyakṣabuddhiḥ svapnādau yathā sā ca yadā tadā
children.translated_text: Perceptual cognition is like that found in dreams and so forth; moreover, when it occurs,

children.text: na so'rtho dṛśyate tasya pratyakṣatvaṃ kathaṃ matam ||
children.translated_text: the object itself is not seen at that moment. How, then, is the cognition considered perceptual?

children.text: uktaṃ yathā tadābhāsā vijñaptiḥ smaraṇaṃ tataḥ
children.translated_text: As already stated, representation appears in the form of that object; memory subsequently arises from it.
One who is not awake does not understand the absence of the object seen in a dream.
Through mutual dominance, representations in different streams reciprocally determine one another.
In a dream the mind is impaired by torpor; therefore its result is not equal to that of waking experience.
Death can arise from a distinctive representation in another's stream, just as transformations
such as loss of memory arise in others through the mental power of <s>piśācas</s> and the like.
Or how else could the emptying of the <s>Daṇḍaka</s> Forest through the anger of sages be explained?

children.text: manodaṇḍo mahāvadyaḥ kathaṃ vā tena sidhyati ||
children.translated_text: And how else could it be established that mental punishment is a particularly grave offense?
How is the cognition of those who know another's mind inaccurate? In the same way as
cognition of one's own mind is inaccurate because of ignorance; its true nature is the domain of the <s>Buddha</s>.
This demonstration of representation-only has been composed by me in accordance with my own capacity;

children.text: kṛteyaṃ sarvathā sā tu na cintyā buddhagocaraḥ ||
children.translated_text: but in its entirety it is inconceivable, for it belongs to the domain of the <s>Buddha</s>.
